thread.title: U.S. Supreme Court Allows Sports Betting: Now What For Investors?

author: Howard Jay Klein
title: U.S. Supreme Court Allows Sports Betting: Now What For Investors?
text:
Investment Thesis: The high court decision on sports betting opens a powerfully bullish set of catalysts for these selected stocks. Beyond immediate spikes on the news, there is a case to be made for further appreciation now as states quickly gear up to initiate legislation.
When once asked by a journalist where all the millions he made as a movie star went, a broke George Raft (1895-1980) replied, "Part of it went on gambling, part of it went on women. The rest I spent foolishly."
That sentiment closely parallels the thinking of millions of Americans who highly value the rush of a good time mixed with expectations of winning by plunking down their shekels on the outcome of a sporting event. They are joined by tens of millions who weekly enhance their pure love of sports or gut loyalties to their alma maters, by betting on or against teams in professional and college sports. Many who have neither the time nor inclination to fly to Vegas to make a lay down on a series of games have for decades migrated to the local bookie who offered fair odds, no limits, and most importantly, credit. With one decision, the US Supreme Court last week, essentially put tens of thousands of bookies as betting options only for deadbeats with shaky credit, old timers, or even newbies in cash businesses. In time, illegal bookies, as they now exist, will essentially see their handle shrink dramatically. The new world of legal sports betting in the USA has arrived, and with it, investing opportunities that now accompany disruptive events in industries with long-established business models. (Photo below: William Hill archive).
The decision: In brief, the high court ruled 6-3 on the juridical principle of states vs. federal rights. The majority opinion was based on the idea that the federal government could not commandeer the individual states to ban sports betting. Neither did it bar the feds from passing some kind of sports betting law on their own, but that is not seen as likely. All states are now free to either legalize sports betting or pass on it.
Who will benefit, who won't? Segment by segment 1. The NCAA and Pro sports leagues: Both the college and pro sports leagues, who have long been opposed to legalization, are already calling for the feds to step in and pass some kind of umbrella law governing essentials like integrity, wagering licensing, etc. That's a thinly disguised expression of the insatiable greed of the leagues to intrude into the coming bonanza. Already league officials are touting what they call the need for one percent "integrity fee" to be paid by the operators on handle to "police" the possibilities of corruption by players or coaches. This, of course, is a patent absurdity, merely another expression of their greed.
We have discussed their possible role with gaming attorneys we've known for decades in both New Jersey and Nevada. In brief, Nevada has never paid a dime's worth of "integrity fees" to any pro or college sports leagues over its many decades of sports wagering business. "It's a very slender reed for the leagues and a dead loser if they go to court." One attorney pointed out that major league baseball, for example, has operated for decades on an anti-trust carve out that functionally bars anyone else from creating a major league team in their individual markets. The other pro leagues get billions out of taxpayer coffers to build stadiums. Pro sports in hand eagle we spoke to. "This will evoke strong legal challenges from designated operators and they'll have powerful cases."
The leagues will benefit from advertising and sponsorship money from the new operators both at the stadium level as well as their TV deals, but that, at least in the opinion of our legal friends, is the extent to which they will share in the take. This is not to say they could be prevented from establishing their own betting sites. But they'd be competing with large public gaming companies with deep pockets, proprietary technological know-how, and marketing savvy. And the leagues, having sat fat, dumb and happy for decades fundamentally without competition, are poorly positioned to prevail in hand to hand marketing combat for bettors. Our take: Their potential in advertising revenue from betting sites could be big enough to slake their revenue thirst in sports betting. (Photo below: Google archive)
2. The banks: The big four credit card issuers have shied away from the gambling credit business until now. We are in new territory though, so do not be surprised to see at some point soon, policy issuance from American Express Company ( AXP ), JPMorgan Chase & Co. ( JPM ), Citi ( C ), and Bank of America Corporation ( BAC ) indicating a new stance if and when sports betting is legalized. With an estimated $150 billion running through the system each year, they can be counted on to find a way to chip off fistfuls of transaction processing pennies for themselves in this area.
3. Casinos: We can expect this sector to be all in on sports betting both in the installation of ever more amenity heavy sports books on their properties as well as running betting sites using their considerable brand values to market their expertise in the area.
Not every company in the sector is all in on the prospect.
Both Wynn Resorts, Ltd. (NASDAQ: WYNN ) and Las Vegas Sands (NYSE: LVS ) have been in turn, lukewarm and outwardly hostile to online sports betting. This could change for Wynn under its new leadership, but in our view, it won't be seen as a mainstream service line. Of the entire sector, we see these companies at the forefront: MGM Resorts International (NYSE: MGM ) is already running a site. Its CEO James J. Murren has been leading the charge for legalization for years.
Also expected to be running hard and fast: Caesars Entertainment Corporation (NASDAQ: CZR ) which likewise runs a site and had broken its online casino business away from its core resort segment during its run in bankruptcy. Its iconic name will be a help. Both MGM and CZR already run sports books at their properties and both run online betting sites in New Jersey, which was the principal petitioner in the landmark case. Other regional operators like Penn National Gaming (NASDAQ: PENN ) which operates some racinos and has a long history in parimutuel wagering.
We also see Churchill Downs (NASDAQ: CHDN ) as a potential big player in the space as it will have a big head start through its TwinSpires online betting site with the flexibility, the database, iconic name value, and prestige to acquire licenses from many states. The problem for investors here is that the stock is already so toppy and its spike since the decision soaring it over $300 a share should keep it in the back burner for investors who will rightfully expect a lot of upside run room on stocks in the sector from now on in. Many stocks in the sector offer far better value if you are betting on sports wagering as a powerhouse catalyst. Churchill's live racing and casino businesses are just okay, nothing to rave about. So, investors will be paying over $300 a share for TwinSpires only. It's natural for a spin off in our view and if it were, we'd call it a buy.
4.The gaming tech operators: This is where we believe the full-frontal attack on the newly born business will be quickest, most aggressive, and in the long run, most successful.
These companies are best positioned to bid for licenses across the US with solid operating histories, deep wells of tech know-how, existing management structures, expertise in erecting firewalls as impregnable as it is possible given the state of the art and transaction processing. Also, to be considered are those with existing relationships with state governments on lottery contracts.
In this group, which has already seen some spiking on the news, we put the following companies we recommend for watch lists and their prices at writing:
Scientific Games Corp. (NASDAQ: SGMS ) $59.55
International Game Technology (NYSE: IGT ) $30.14
The Stars Group, Inc. (NASDAQ: TSG ) $36.67
William Hill plc ( OTCPK:WIMHY ). Note: William Hill currently runs sports books at Nevada casinos. Their UK-based business includes their legacy street side betting shops as well as a huge online business.
5. The cable/fantasy sports entrants: The two big fantasy sports sites, DraftKings and FanDuel are expected to reinstate their efforts to go public, either merged or individually. Their databases give them a good leg up, but they have had problems convincing many regulators that their firewalls and betting pool protection technology are top notch. If they don't go public, they'll be bought. But they will be in race.
6. TV/digital operators: We will hear from the likes of Yahoo, Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), and Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ). More likely than not they could opt to buy into the business rather than attempting to reinvent the wheel. Yet given their massive capacity to innovate and create digital platforms that are super user-friendly, they can't be counted out.
The Takeaway: There is little question that the court decision has overnight created the basis of a multi-billion-dollar industry that will disrupt the US gaming and wagering scene in a way even bigger than the 1978 legalization of casinos in Atlantic City. What faces investors now is a process of separating the dozens upon dozens of pretenders from the crop of serious competitors for up to 32 state licenses that should come up for bidding within the next five years or less. SA readers interested in the sector should check out our SA marketplace site, The House Edge for more detailed research on the birth of this new sector in gaming.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
